title: Bound on a finite group acting on valued-field initial forms
statement:
Let $F\subseteq E$ be a finite extension of fields [def-weil-field] with compatible real-valued nonarchimedean absolute values: $|x|=0$ iff $x=0$, $|xy|=|x||y|$, $|1|=1$ and $|x+y|\le\max(|x|,|y|)$. For $D=F,E$ put $D^\circ=\{x:|x|\le1\}$ [def-trf-valuation-ring], $\mathfrak m_D=\{x:|x|<1\}$, $k_D=D^\circ/\mathfrak m_D$, and $\Gamma_D=|D^\times|$. Assume $e=|\Gamma_E/\Gamma_F|$ and $f=[k_E:k_F]$ are finite. Let $p=\operatorname{char}(k_F)$, and let $e'$ be the largest divisor of $e$ prime to $p$ if $p>0$, and $e'=e$ if $p=0$. Fix an algebraic closure $\Omega$ of $k_F$ [def-weil-algebraic-closure], and let $s$ be the number of $k_F$-field embeddings $k_E\hookrightarrow\Omega$. Let $H$ be any finite subgroup of $\operatorname{Aut}_F(E)$ such that $|h(x)|=|x|$ for all $h\in H,x\in E$, and define
$$Q=\{h\in H:|h(x)-x|<|x|\text{ for every }x\ne0\}.$$
Then $Q$ is a normal subgroup of $H$, $1\le s\le f$, and
$$[H:Q]\le e's.$$
Moreover $s=f$ if and only if $k_E/k_F$ is separable, meaning that every minimal polynomial over $k_F$ of an element of $k_E$ has distinct roots. Neither completeness, discreteness, normality of $E/F$, nor perfection of $k_F$ is assumed.

proof.text: For $D=F,E$, the norm identities show that $D^\circ$ is a subring and $\mathfrak m_D$ a proper ideal. Every element outside $\mathfrak m_D$ in $D^\circ$ has norm $1$, so its inverse lies in $D^\circ$; hence $k_D$ is a field. For nonzero $x$, either $x$ or $x^{-1}$ belongs to $D^\circ$, as required by [def-trf-valuation-ring]. Compatibility gives $F^\circ=F\cap E^\circ$ and $\mathfrak m_F=F\cap\mathfrak m_E$, so the residue map $k_F\to k_E$ is injective. Each $h\in H$ preserves $E^\circ$ and $\mathfrak m_E$ and therefore induces $\bar h(\bar x)=\overline{h(x)}$. This is well-defined because $|x-y|<1$ implies $|h(x)-h(y)|<1$. Its inverse is induced by $h^{-1}$; composition and fixation of $k_F$ follow on representatives. Put $\rho(h)=\bar h$ and $I=\ker\rho$.

proof.text: The identity lies in $Q$. For $q,t\in Q$ and $x\ne0$, write $qt(x)-x=q(t(x)-x)+(q(x)-x)$; the ultrametric inequality and isometry give norm strictly below $|x|$. Also $|q^{-1}(x)-x|=|x-q(x)|<|x|$. Thus $Q$ is a subgroup. For $g\in H$, $$|gqg^{-1}(x)-x|=|q(g^{-1}x)-g^{-1}x|<|g^{-1}x|=|x|,$$ so $Q$ is normal in $H$. Finally, for $a\in E^\circ\setminus\{0\}$ and $q\in Q$, $|q(a)-a|<|a|\le1$; the case $a=0$ is automatic. Hence $q$ fixes every residue class and $Q\subseteq I$.

source.place: Section 6.2.8, pairing (6.2.9), PDF p.209, printed p.207. Agent writes the well-definedness, composition and kernel calculations for an arbitrary finite isometric group; the source assumes a henselian base and a Galois extension, which are not invoked here.

proof.text: Write $A=\Gamma_E/\Gamma_F$. For $h\in I$ and $x\in E^\times$, the element $h(x)/x$ has norm $1$, so its residue $c_h(x)$ belongs to $k_E^\times$. If $|y|=|x|$, put $u=y/x$, a unit of norm $1$. Then $$c_h(y)c_h(x)^{-1}=\overline{h(u)/u}=1$$ because $h$ fixes the residue of $u$. Thus $c_h(x)$ depends only on $|x|$. Moreover $c_h(xy)=c_h(x)c_h(y)$; and for $a\in F^\times$, $h(a)=a$, so $c_h(a)=1$. Consequently the rule $\chi_h([|x|])=c_h(x)$ is a well-defined homomorphism $A\to k_E^\times$: replacing $x$ by an element whose norm differs by $|a|$ reduces to the equal-norm calculation after multiplication by $a$.

source.place: Section 6.2.8, pairing (6.2.9), PDF p.209, printed p.207. Agent writes the well-definedness, composition and kernel calculations for an arbitrary finite isometric group; the source assumes a henselian base and a Galois extension, which are not invoked here.

proof.text: For $h,t\in I$ one has $$\frac{ht(x)}x=h\!\left(\frac{t(x)}x\right)\frac{h(x)}x.$$ The first factor is a norm-one unit, and $h$ acts trivially on its residue. Reducing gives $\chi_{ht}=\chi_h\chi_t$, hence a group homomorphism $\chi:I\to\operatorname{Hom}(A,k_E^\times)$. Its kernel is exactly $Q$: for every $x\ne0$, $$\chi_h([|x|])=1\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \left|\frac{h(x)}x-1\right|<1\ \Longleftrightarrow\ |h(x)-x|<|x|.$$ Here equality to $1$ in the residue field means that the difference from $1$ is in $\mathfrak m_E$.

source.place: Section 6.2.8, pairing (6.2.9), PDF p.209, printed p.207. Agent writes the well-definedness, composition and kernel calculations for an arbitrary finite isometric group; the source assumes a henselian base and a Galois extension, which are not invoked here.

proof.text: The group $A$ is finite abelian of order $e$ by hypothesis. The embedding $k_F\hookrightarrow k_E$ gives $\operatorname{char}(k_E)=p$, since an integer multiple of $1$ vanishes in one field precisely when it vanishes in the other. Apply [lem-trf-finite-abelian-character-prime-bound] to $A$ and $k_E$. Its prime-to-characteristic part of $|A|$ is the stated $e'$, including the convention when $p=0$. Therefore $\operatorname{Hom}(A,k_E^\times)$ is finite with at most $e'$ elements.

source.place: Section 6.2.8, pairing (6.2.9), PDF p.209, printed p.207. Agent writes the well-definedness, composition and kernel calculations for an arbitrary finite isometric group; the source assumes a henselian base and a Galois extension, which are not invoked here.

proof.text: Apply [lem-trf-finite-embedding-separability-count] to the finite extension $k_E/k_F$ of degree $f$ and the specified algebraic closure $\Omega$. It gives $s\ge1$ and $s=f$ exactly when $k_E/k_F$ is separable, in the stated minimal-polynomial sense. The existing bound [lem-weil-pbc-finite-extension-finitely-many-embeddings] gives $s\le f$. Fix one such embedding $j:k_E\hookrightarrow\Omega$. The map $\rho(H)\to\operatorname{Hom}_{k_F\text{-alg}}(k_E,\Omega)$, $\alpha\mapsto j\circ\alpha$, is injective: equality of the composites implies equality of $\alpha$ by injectivity of $j$. Thus $|\rho(H)|\le s$.

source.place: Tags 09HA (lemma-separable-equality) and 09H8 (lemma-count-embeddings-explicitly); postcomposition injection written out.

proof.text: Count the fibres of the two homomorphisms. If $h_0\in H$, then $\rho(h)=\rho(h_0)$ exactly when $h_0^{-1}h\in I$; thus the fibre is the coset $h_0I$, in bijection with $I$. Therefore $|H|=|\rho(H)||I|$. Likewise, since $\ker\chi=Q$, each nonempty fibre of $\chi$ is a coset of $Q$, giving $|I|=|\chi(I)||Q|$. Finally the cosets of $Q$ partition $H$ into sets of size $|Q|$, so $[H:Q]|Q|=|H|$. The positive integer $|Q|$ cancels, giving $$[H:Q]=|\rho(H)|\,|\chi(I)|\le s\,e'=e' s.$$ The two bounds are Steps 5 and 6. Along with Steps 2 and 6 this gives all conclusions. These are finite-set partitions and multiplication bijections, with no normality or separability assumption on the valued extension.
